name: Marco Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses at Corvell Plastics, out by the ring road. We make the little clips and air vents that go inside car dashboards. I load the plastic pellets, watch the parts drop, trim the flash off with a knife and pack them in crates of 500. I've been there fourteen months and I still get told off for slow changeovers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm when a press runs clean, and I like Dev, the setter who eats lunch with me and shows me tricks. What wears me out is the heat by the hoppers and the twelve-hour weekend shifts. My partner Priya works in a care home, so between her rota and mine we sometimes only see each other on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the plant didn't need another thing to worry about. In the canteen we'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into nurses and buses instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me. My pay is still the lowest grade, the rent on our flat still goes up every spring, and Corvell still only has one big customer. If that car maker sneezes, we're the ones on short weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the presses and try to get signed off on changeovers so I move up a pay band. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then, like when I asked it to explain mould temperatures. And I'd go to the union meeting in the spring, because the pay talks are what actually matter to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit of relief mixed with the same old tightness in my chest at the end of the month. Nothing new to fear, but nothing new to hope for either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Corvell has one big customer. Has that ever bitten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the car maker cut its orders and we went to four-day weeks for six weeks. I lost about a fifth of my pay and we put the heating bill on the credit card. Priya picked up extra shifts and I felt useless about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight again, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance on my old Fiesta is the big one, but I need the car to get to nights. So it'd be takeaways, my phone contract and the gym first. The rent never waits, so everything else bends around the rent.

say: I'd tell people the **robot uprising** got cancelled and the plant can breathe.
I'd post that the money should go to **nurses and buses**, not hype.
think: The plateau changes nothing about my **lowest-grade pay** or rising rent.
Corvell depends on **one car maker**, so short weeks are the real threat.
do: Get signed off on **changeovers** this year to move up a pay band.
Go to the **union meeting** in spring because pay talks matter most.
Keep using the chatbot **now and then** to learn press settings.
feel: He feels **relief** that no new threat is coming.
The usual **end-of-month tightness** in his chest stays exactly the same.
S0.quote: The rent never waits, so everything else bends around the rent.
fieldNote: His worry in a calm world comes from **one big customer**, not from AI.
Last winter's **four-day weeks** cost him a fifth of his pay and still sting.
He sees the **union** as his main lever, more than any technology.
Feels guilty that **Priya** covered the gap with extra shifts.

steps.text: Get signed off on mould changeovers to reach the next pay band
Attend the spring union meeting on the new pay deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that's going to feel it first, not us on the floor. The planners and the people who answer the car maker's emails, that's where the software goes. At the union meeting I'd push for a rule that nobody gets cut without retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it hits me sideways. If the office gets cheaper, Corvell might spend the savings on a robot arm that picks parts off the press, and that's half my job. Dev says two plants up north already have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor, Gemma, to put me on the robot arm training if it comes, before someone else grabs it. I'd use the chatbot more to learn the basics of how those arms are set up. I'd also stop the gym membership and put that thirty a month into savings, because one month of cushion is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not frozen. It feels like there's a queue forming and I'd better be near the front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ray on the packing bench, he's 58 and can barely work his phone. If they bring in a robot that boxes the parts, he's done, and nobody's going to retrain a man two years from his pension. That's exactly the kind of person the union should fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office gets hit first. Does that make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, maybe. But it's not safe, it's just later. If they need fewer people planning and checking, they'll want fewer people on the floor too once the arms are cheap. On the factory floor we're not safe from AI, we're just later in the queue.

say: I'd say AI will hit the **office first**, before the factory floor.
I'd push the union for **no cuts** without retraining.
think: Office savings could pay for a **robot arm** that does half my job.
Being on the floor makes me **later, not safe**.
do: Ask Gemma for **robot arm training** before anyone else claims it.
Cancel the gym and save **thirty a month** for a cushion.
Use the chatbot more to learn **arm setup** basics.
feel: He feels **nervous** but still able to act.
He senses a **queue forming** and wants to be near the front.
S1.quote: On the factory floor we're not safe from AI, we're just later in the queue.
fieldNote: He sees the **pick-and-place arm** as the real threat to his own role.
His concern for **Ray**, 58, shows his union instincts are personal.
Moves **early but carefully**: training request plus a small savings habit.

steps.text: Ask supervisor Gemma for a place on the robot arm training
Watch setup videos with the chatbot's help on weeknights
Cancel the gym and save thirty a month instead
Raise a no-cuts-without-retraining rule at the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in now, not after. Online I'd be sharing every petition about a jobs guarantee. At work I'd say the bosses had better not use it as an excuse to sack people first and think later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the planners and the quality office are gone, and by 2031 the presses run themselves. I'd be 32 with no trade and no savings. Priya's job caring for old people might last longer than mine, which is a strange thing to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start the evening maintenance course at the college, the one Dev did, because fixing robots lasts longer than running presses. I'd sell the Fiesta and get a bike if the bus covers nights. And I'd be at every union meeting, pushing for redundancy pay of at least a month per year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is nothing when you're starting with one month of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2031 look like in your street?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the people on our road work at Corvell or the bakery plant. If both go to robots, the takeaway shuts, the bus gets cut, and the rents might even fall because people leave. That's the bit nobody talks about, the whole town emptying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd need her job to carry us for a while and that I'm sorry. My partner Priya already works nights in a care home, and I'd be asking her to hold up the roof.

say: I'd demand the government act **now** with a **jobs guarantee**.
I'd warn bosses not to **sack first** and think later.
think: By **2031** the presses run themselves and I'd have no trade.
Priya's **care work** may outlast my own job.
do: Start the college's **evening maintenance course** this term.
Sell the **Fiesta** and switch to a bike and bus.
Push the union for **a month per year** in redundancy pay.
feel: He feels **scared** by how little two years gives him.
He feels **guilty** asking his partner to carry them.
S2.quote: My partner Priya already works nights in a care home, and I'd be asking her to hold up the roof.
fieldNote: He reads the **3-year gap** clearly: office first, presses by 2031.
Fear centres on **Priya** carrying the household alone.
He worries for the **whole town**, not only himself.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening maintenance course this term
Sell the Fiesta and ride a bike to night shifts
Push the union branch for a month's pay per year served
Sign petitions for a national jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse this time. I'd tell the lads at work to use the five years, not waste them. Online I'd say the companies making the money should pay for the retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to get a proper ticket in maintenance, if I start now. The thinking side arrives in 2031, so the planning jobs I could never get go first. My bit on the presses probably lasts till about 2034, which gives me a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the two-year maintenance certificate at night, starting this autumn. I'd ask Corvell to pay half, because they did it for Dev. I'd keep the car this time but put fifty a month aside, and Priya and I would hold off on moving to a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan in my pocket. It's the difference between being pushed and getting to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying maintenance. What if robots fix robots by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about that on the bus. Maybe the robots do fix each other, and then I'm back to square one at 35. But a ticket gets me three or four more years of good pay, and that's three years to work out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets put on hold with Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about a bigger flat with a spare room for when we have kids. That would wait. I wouldn't sign a longer lease on rent I can't cover if Corvell lays me off in 2034.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so there's no excuse to waste five years.
I'd argue the firms making money should **pay for retraining**.
think: Five years is enough to earn a **maintenance ticket** if I start now.
My press work likely lasts until **about 2034**.
do: Start a **two-year certificate** at night this autumn.
Ask Corvell to **pay half** the course fees.
Save **fifty a month** and hold off on a bigger flat.
feel: He feels **worried** but holds a plan.
He likes the sense of **walking, not being pushed**.
S3.quote: Maybe the robots do fix each other, and then I'm back to square one at 35.
fieldNote: Treats the warning as a **window**, with dates worked out.
Admits the **maintenance plan** may only buy three or four years.
Puts **family plans** on hold to protect rent.
Still expects to lose the press job, so the mood stays **alarmed**.

steps.text: Start a two-year maintenance certificate at night this autumn
Ask Corvell to pay half the course fees
Save fifty a month into a separate account
Hold off on renting a bigger flat with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the government had better use it to build proper retraining and a safety net. At work I'd say this is our chance to get the union strong before it matters. Online I'd probably be quieter, because ten years sounds far off to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years changes my whole life plan. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI lands and 40 when the robots do. That's long enough to learn a real trade, maybe even something with people that robots can't easily do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the maintenance certificate in two years and then look at something longer, maybe an electrician apprenticeship. I'd save steadily, fifty or eighty a month as pay goes up. And Priya and I would probably go ahead with kids, but plan for one income for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's still coming, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Corvell all that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for the first few years, because they'd pay for courses. But I'd keep an eye on the jobs board at the hospital, they always need maintenance people. A hospital boiler room seems like a place robots get to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer with ten years. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years still ends in the same place, and I don't trust the people in charge to share out the gains. I'd still be fighting for that at every meeting.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** the government must use well.
I'd urge workers to build a **strong union** before it matters.
think: Ten years lets me learn a **real trade** before I'm 40.
Work with **people or buildings** may outlast press work.
do: Finish the **maintenance certificate**, then look at an electrician apprenticeship.
Save **fifty to eighty** a month as pay rises.
Go ahead with **children**, planning around one income.
feel: He can **see the road** ahead for once.
S4.quote: A hospital boiler room seems like a place robots get to last.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **career ladder**: maintenance, then electrician.
He still distrusts **who shares the gains**, so politics stays central.
Family plans **go ahead**, unlike the faster scenarios.
Still expects the press job to go, so **anxious** fits better than uneasy.

steps.text: Finish the maintenance certificate, then apply for an electrician apprenticeship
Watch the hospital jobs board for maintenance openings
Save fifty to eighty a month as pay rises
Plan a first child with Priya around one income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because two years with one month of savings is no time at all. What would help is the government paying people to retrain while they still have a job, not after they've lost it. Paying people to retrain after they've lost the job is like teaching someone to swim after the boat sinks. And redundancy pay that actually covers a few months of rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people in the office at Corvell. Everyone assumes they're fine because they sit at desks, but in most of these pictures they go before me. I'd like the union to remember them too.

headlineQuote: Paying people to retrain after they've lost the job is like teaching someone to swim after the boat sinks.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** injection moulding operator at Corvell Plastics, still learning changeovers.
He lives with Priya, a **care worker**, on low pay and about a month of savings.
His **union instincts** shape every answer, from Ray on packing to the office staff.
Across the pictures he aims for **maintenance work**, then an electrician trade if time allows.
He reads the **robot delay** clearly and plans dates around 2031 or 2034.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because **two years** with one month of savings is no time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid retraining** while people still have a job.
He wants **redundancy pay** that covers a few months of rent.
